title: The 1806 Interior Expeditions · Zalvidea & Moraga
subtitle: The Zalvidea and Munoz diaries, stop by stop, with Cook's identifications and the disagreements between them
abstract: Two probes into the Central Valley in 1806: Fr. Jose Maria de Zalvidea from Santa Barbara through the southern valley to San Gabriel in July and August, and Gabriel Moraga with Fr. Pedro Munoz from San Juan Bautista up the San Joaquin and back down the foothills to San Fernando from September to November. Each stop carries the diary's own account of the day and the identification Cook made of the place in 1960. Routes are reconstructed from the diaries' leagues and bearings; village pins are approximate, and the ones Cook declined to locate are marked as guesses.

features.name: Mission Santa Ynez
features.summary: Founded 1804. Zalvidea reached it on the evening of 19 July 1806 and left it on the 20th.

features.name: Mission San Gabriel
features.summary: Founded 1771. Zalvidea arrival.

features.summary: Founded 1797. Moraga departure point.

features.name: Mission San Fernando
features.summary: Founded 1797. Moraga arrival.

features.name: Jonatas
features.summary: Cook places Jonatas at Las Olivas, the present Los Olivos. Zalvidea found only the remains of the village, three leagues north of Santa Ynez, 20 July 1806.

features.name: Sgene
features.summary: In the lower Cuyama Valley, T 10 N, R 25 W. Seven men, sixteen women and three children.

features.name: Malapoa (Hoschiu)
features.summary: Placed by Gifford and Schenck on Bitterwater Creek and identified by them with Hoschiu, of the Yokuts tribe Tulamni. Twenty-nine men, twenty-two women and eight children. The diary puts Malapoa seven leagues east of Sgene, which does not agree with that placement.

features.name: Buenavista (Tilamniu)
features.summary: Identified by Gifford and Schenck with Tilamniu, which Kroeber puts on the western or north-western end of Buena Vista Lake. The Indians gave its numbers as thirty-six men, 144 women and thirty-eight children.

features.name: Sisupistu (Pohalin Tinliu)
features.summary: Considered to be Pohalin Tinliu, at the south-east corner of Kern Lake. Zalvidea counted twenty-eight houses and saw fifty to sixty men; most of the people were away harvesting.

sources.citation: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 5.

features.name: Tupai
features.summary: The name of Zalvidea's camp. Placed doubtfully by Gifford and Schenck at Tejon Ranch on El Paso Creek.

features.name: Tacui (Tecuya)
features.summary: Undoubtedly Tecuya, on Tecuya Creek. Twenty-three souls.

features.name: Yaguelame (Woilo)
features.summary: The village of the rivers, nine leagues north of Tecuya on the Kern River. Gifford and Schenck proposed either Loasau or Woilo; Cook prefers Woilo, because Loasau was on Kern Lake rather than the river and Woilo is very close to nine leagues from Tecuya. Zalvidea counted ninety-two men aged seven to forty and reckoned the village at 300 souls.

features.name: Taslupi
features.summary: Placed by Gifford and Schenck on Tejon Creek, which fits the distances; Cook thinks Pastoria on Grapevine Creek more likely. Five houses, standing empty in August 1806.

features.name: Casteque (Castaic)
features.summary: At the head of Grapevine Creek. Empty when Zalvidea reached it on 7 August 1806: the people were away at their fields of Guata.

features.name: Atongai
features.summary: A Serrano village of thirty-two men, thirty-six women and fifteen children, with a swamp a league and a half off. Cook does not locate it; the pin follows the diary's four leagues west of Guapiabit and is a guess.

features.name: Guapiabit
features.summary: Nineteen men, sixteen women and eleven children; the expedition rested here on 12 August 1806 and this was its easternmost point. The pin follows the diary's four leagues east of Moscopiabit and is a guess.

features.name: Moscopiabit (Muscupian)
features.summary: Fifteen to eighteen adults and a few children. Cutter identifies the Muscupian of a later expedition with Zalvidea's Moscopiabit, in the vicinity of Cajon Pass; this is the only published fix among the eastern villages.

sources.citation: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925).

Cutter's identification of Moscopiabit is reported at Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. IV n. 3.

features.name: Guapiana
features.summary: The last village of the journey, by a watering place, where children from San Gabriel were found. Cook does not locate it; the pin follows the diary's leagues and is a guess.

sources.citation: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 12.

features.name: Nupchenche
features.summary: About 250 souls under a chief called Choley, on the far bank of the San Joaquin among willows. Cook places it on the east bank in T 11 S, R 14 E, far more than the three leagues from camp the diary gives, and counts it among the lower San Joaquin villages effaced so thoroughly that modern informants gave ethnographers no indication they had ever existed. The pin follows the diary's three leagues and is a guess.

III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 17.

features.name: Taulamne (Tahualamne)
features.summary: A village on cliffs the party could not climb, whose people lived in caves. Schenck places Taulamne on an inaccessible rock on the Stanislaus in the foothills, and distinguishes it from Taualames at the ford of the San Joaquin below the mouth of the Tuolumne; Kroeber lists a Lakisamni rancheria at Dent's or Knights Ferry. Cook leaves the people either Miwok or Yokuts, the language boundary running near by, and notes that the villages higher up the river must have been Central Miwok. Tahualamne is the form in the diary's own village list.

sources.citation: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 24.

features.name: Chineguis
features.summary: The Merced village where an old woman was baptized on 29 September 1806. Near by were Yunate, Chamuasi, Latelate and Lachuo. Cook counts a minimum of six villages in this stretch of the river, averaging about 225 souls.

sources.citation: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 19.

features.name: Pizcache (Pitkachi)
features.summary: About 200 souls under a chief named Sujoyucomu. The diary places the village farther in the interior of the mountains, on the bank of the San Joaquin; Kroeber has the Pitkachi on the south side of the river at Kohuou near Herndon or Sycamore, at Weshiu on a slough, and at Gewachiu farther downstream, and Cook infers from Gayton that the group moved downstream between 1806 and 1850. The pin follows the diary.

sources.citation: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III, who reports the placements of Gifford and Schenck (1926) and Kroeber, Handbook of the Indians of California (1925), chap. III n. 28.

features.name: Telame (Telamni)
features.summary: The large village of the Kaweah delta, about 600 souls, where twenty-two people were baptized in October 1806. These are the Telamni of the ethnographers, repeatedly mentioned by the early explorers. Munoz put the population of the lower Kaweah at 3,000; Cook holds the true figure was probably much higher.

sources.citation: Village identifications from Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. stops.name: Santa Barbara
stops.summary: Setting out. The expedition left Santa Barbara on the morning of 19 July 1806 to carry out the Governor's orders, contained in his official letter of the 10th of that month, and reached Mission Santa Ynez the same afternoon. The diary says only Santa Barbara, without distinguishing the presidio from the mission.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

stops.name: Mission Santa Ynez
stops.summary: Departure north. The party left Santa Ynez after Mass on 20 July 1806 and travelled north.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

stops.name: Jonatas (Las Olivas)
stops.summary: The remains of the village of Jonatas, three leagues north of the mission. Cook places it at Las Olivas, the present Los Olivos. His identifications here compress the diary's three-league intervals.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

stops.name: Saca (Alamo Pintado Creek)
stops.summary: Saca, three leagues beyond Jonatas, whose people were Christians of Santa Ynez. Cook places it on Alamo Pintado Creek.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

stops.name: Olomosong (Sisquoc River)
stops.summary: Olomosong, five leagues on, a village of three houses holding two old women and four young women with the chief. Zalvidea baptized the two old women, of eighty and seventy years. Cook: probably on the Sisquoc River near the 120th meridian.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

stops.name: Gecp (south slope, Sierra Madre)
stops.summary: Gecp, four leagues north: five houses, four men and seven women, two old women baptized. The road ran through broken mountains and the party slept in a valley with a small stream. Cook puts it apparently on the south slope of the Sierra Madre, because the next day they climbed a mountain and came out onto plains, which he takes for the Cuyama Valley at about T 10 N, R 28 W.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

stops.name: Talihuilimit
stops.summary: Talihuilimit, two leagues east across the plains, perhaps twenty-five people. Three old women baptized, one with a paralysed leg, one bitten in the hip by a bear, one reckoned over a hundred years old; two had Christian sons at Santa Ynez and La Purisima.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 1.

stops.name: Lisahua (Salisbury Canyon)
stops.summary: Lisahua, six leagues east: twenty-eight people, five baptized. A stream like the one at Mission San Fernando ran near by; the land was arid and saline, without grass or timber. Cook: probably in lower Salisbury Canyon, T 9 N, R 26 W.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 2.

stops.name: Cuia (lower Santa Barbara Canyon)
stops.summary: Cuia, four leagues east: nine houses, fourteen men, nineteen women, eight children, seven baptized. Three small springs near by. Four leagues south lay Siguecin, with ten men, nineteen women and a few children, where two more were baptized; Cook puts Siguecin twelve to fifteen miles up the canyon to the south. The party returned to sleep at Lisahua. Cook: Cuia may have been in lower Santa Barbara Canyon, T 9 N, R 25 W.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 2.

stops.name: Sgene (lower Cuyama Valley)
stops.summary: Sgene, reached after a salt marsh, a cross made of logs and a wild horse: seven men, sixteen women, three children, four baptized. Cook: the party evidently bore more to the north, somewhere in the lower Cuyama Valley, T 10 N, R 25 W.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 3.

stops.name: Malapoa (Bitterwater Creek)
stops.summary: Malapoa, which the diary puts seven leagues east of Sgene: twenty-nine men, twenty-two women, eight children, one old woman baptized. Gifford and Schenck place it on Bitterwater Creek and identify it with Hoschiu, of the Yokuts tribe Tulamni; that placement lies north-west of Sgene rather than seven leagues east of it, and the pin follows Gifford and Schenck. Cook adds that all the preceding villages were Tokya Chumash. That afternoon Zalvidea rode with the Lieutenant to a small settlement of the village of Napolea, which Cook (as Nopalea) places on either Bitterwater or Santiago Creek, and baptized six more.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 4.

stops.name: Buenavista (Tilamniu)
stops.summary: Buenavista, eight leagues north, on the shore of a lake the diary calls eight leagues long and five wide, with rafts on the water and a river that divided into three branches and rejoined to form it. The Indians gave its numbers as thirty-six men, 144 women and thirty-eight children; one old woman of ninety was baptized. The party slept two leagues off. Gifford and Schenck identify the village with Tilamniu, which Kroeber puts on the western or north-western end of the lake.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 5.

stops.name: Sisupistu (Pohalin Tinliu)
stops.summary: Sisupistu, at the end of the lake, reached at dark on 26 July after a day east along the shore and then north. The arrival nearly caused a fight: the villagers fled into a tule swamp and their warriors threw a spear at the chief of the Buenavista party, who were their enemies. Zalvidea talked the two chiefs into peace, collected the Buenavista bows and arrows for the night and returned them in the morning. He counted twenty-eight houses and saw fifty to sixty men. Cook identifies the village with Pohalin Tinliu at the south-east corner of Kern Lake, and the big river as the Kern.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 5.

stops.name: Camp at Tupai (Tejon or El Paso Creek)
stops.summary: The camp, pitched on 27 July at the edge of the foothills with the intention of staying several days to explore, and held for a week. On the way in, an old woman was found dying alone in a hut; Zalvidea baptized her and she died two hours later. The diary gives the place name as Tupai. The reconnaissance of 28 July worked the lower courses of El Paso, Tejon and Pastoria creeks, five streams in all, and Zalvidea judged the surrounding plains, which he thought larger than those of Mission Santa Clara, able to carry twelve thousand head of cattle. Cook: six leagues from Sisupistu would have brought the party to the mouth of either Tejon or El Paso Creek, and Gifford and Schenck place Tupai doubtfully at Tejon Ranch on El Paso Creek.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 6.

stops.name: Tacui (Tecuya Creek)
stops.summary: Tacui, twenty-three souls, two old men baptized, reached on a day ride with the Sergeant, Corporal and seven soldiers past the stream running out of Grapevine Canyon. Cook: the party apparently doubled back west past Grapevine Creek to Tacui, which was undoubtedly Tecuya on Tecuya Creek.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 7.

stops.name: Yaguelame (Woilo), the village of the rivers
stops.summary: The village of the rivers, Yaguelame, reached on 1 August after two days north. Zalvidea counted ninety-two men between seven and forty years old and reckoned the village at 300 souls; he measured the two river branches at sixteen yards by one and seven yards by a third of a yard, and was told of thirteen villages of the Bald Indians two days to the north, all offering themselves for baptism if missions were founded. Some chiefs asked him, in his report, why the missions were not established without delay. Cook puts Yaguelame nine leagues north of Tecuya on the Kern River; Gifford and Schenck proposed either Loasau or Woilo, and Cook prefers Woilo, since Loasau was on Kern Lake rather than the river and Woilo is very close to nine leagues from Tecuya.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 8.

stops.name: Eastern end of Kern Lake
stops.summary: The end of the lake, passed on the afternoon of 3 August on the way south; the party stopped a league beyond. Cook places it at the eastern end of Kern Lake, T 32 S, R 28 E.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 9.

stops.name: Taslupi (Pastoria or Tejon Creek)
stops.summary: Taslupi, a village of five houses standing empty, at the entrance of a canyon where the Indians had killed two soldiers some years before. Gifford and Schenck place Taslupi on Tejon Creek, which fits the distances; Cook thinks Pastoria on Grapevine Creek more likely, since the party reached Castaic at the head of Grapevine Creek on 7 August.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 10.

stops.name: Casteque (Castaic), head of Grapevine Creek
stops.summary: Casteque, visited on 7 August with the Sergeant and seven soldiers. No one was there: the people were all away at their fields of Guata. Cook names the place Castaic, at the head of Grapevine Creek.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 10.

stops.name: Antelope Valley
stops.summary: The wide valley entered on 8 August, which Cook identifies as Antelope Valley. The diary calls it sixteen leagues long with no watering place in the whole expanse; the party crossed it eastward on 9 August, camped by a gully with plenty of water, and spent 10 August in the hills adjacent to the mountains, passing the remains of a village and a few wells.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 11.

stops.name: Atongai
stops.summary: Atongai, reached after seven leagues east on 11 August: thirty-two men, thirty-six women, fifteen children, with a swamp a league and a half off, pine forests in sight and land that would yield grain if watered. Zalvidea baptized two old men and three old women here. Cook does not locate the villages of this eastern leg, noting only that the party saw several Serrano villages well beyond the limits of the San Joaquin Valley; the pin is placed four leagues west of Guapiabit, as the diary gives the interval, and is a guess.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

stops.name: Guapiabit
stops.summary: Guapiabit, four leagues on, where the expedition rested through 12 August: nineteen men, sixteen women, eleven children, with a pine-covered hill two leagues off, a well and ground moist enough for crops. Three old women and two old men were baptized. This was the easternmost point of the journey. The pin is placed four leagues east of Moscopiabit and is a guess; only Moscopiabit in this group carries a published identification.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

stops.name: Moscopiabit (vicinity of Cajon Pass)
stops.summary: Moscopiabit, four leagues west of Guapiabit, where fifteen to eighteen adults and a few children were seen and two old women baptized. Cutter identifies the Muscupian of a later expedition with Zalvidea's Moscopiabit, in the vicinity of Cajon Pass, which is the only published fix on this leg of the route.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

Cutter's identification of Moscopiabit is reported at Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. IV n. 3.

stops.name: Camp on a stream running to the Santa Ana
stops.summary: Four leagues west of Moscopiabit the party found a village of five houses standing empty, and two leagues beyond it a big stream which, Zalvidea was told, runs into the Santa Ana River. They camped a short distance from it. The pin follows those leagues west from Cajon Pass and is a guess.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

stops.name: Guapiana
stops.summary: Guapiana, the last village of the journey, by a watering place six leagues on. Children from San Gabriel were there; Zalvidea baptized an old woman and named her Gabriela. Earlier that morning he had baptized a very old man found on the trail who could not name his village. The pin follows the diary's leagues west and is a guess.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

stops.name: Mission San Gabriel
stops.summary: Arrival. The party entered San Gabriel on the night of 14 August 1806, and Zalvidea signed the report there. Cook: the party crossed the mountains and went south-west to the mission, having seen several Serrano villages in country well beyond the limits of the San Joaquin Valley.

sources.citation: Zalvidea, Report of an expedition to the interior, 19 July to 14 August 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 49-68, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 12.

routes.notes: The line joins the places Cook names in his footnotes to Zalvidea's report, in diary order. Cook stops locating the villages once the party passes east of Antelope Valley, so the last four days are drawn from the diary's leagues and bearings alone and are marked as guesses.

routes.label: Moraga and Munoz, northbound (21 September to 4 October 1806)
routes.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

stops.name: Mission San Juan Bautista
stops.summary: Departure. On the morning of the first day the troops were given a formal address on the purpose of the expedition, and the party left the mission at about two o'clock in the afternoon. Fr. Pedro Munoz went as chaplain and kept the diary; Gabriel Moraga, second lieutenant of the San Francisco company, commanded, under orders from Governor Jose Joaquin de Arrillaga.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

stops.name: Huzaymas, camp on the San Benito River
stops.summary: A league and a half east across a well forage plain to a creek the diary calls that of the Huzaymas, well grown with alders and oaks, dry in summer. Cook: the camp was on the San Benito River, a league and a half from San Juan Bautista, not on Pacheco Creek as Cutter had it.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 13.

stops.name: San Luis Ranch, Pacheco Pass
stops.summary: The second day's camp, made in the discomfort of three showers. Cook: approximately at San Luis Ranch, where Highway 152 crosses San Luis Creek.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 14.

stops.name: Santa Rita camp
stops.summary: The camp at Santa Rita, with black willow along the stream. Cook puts it fifteen to twenty miles east of San Luis Gonzaga and five or six miles west of the main San Joaquin, on Salt Slough or Paso Slough a few miles north-east of Los Banos, and warns that the sloughs and the channels of the San Joaquin are hard to place on a modern map because of a century of drainage and reclamation. On the fourth day a party rode south to a village reported to hold 400 people and found it empty.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 15.

stops.name: Camp on the San Joaquin
stops.summary: The camp moved to the San Joaquin, about two leagues from Santa Rita. Beaver and salmon abounded, by the account of the local Indians. That afternoon forty-two warriors came in, friendly, brought a little fish, were shown an image of Our Lady of Sorrows and stayed the night in camp. Cook: the camp may be assumed to lie in T 8 S, R 11 E.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 16.

stops.name: Nupchenche
stops.summary: Nupchenche, about three leagues off on the far side of the river, hidden among willows: about 250 souls under a chief called Choley. An old woman came out and sprinkled the party with seeds; the chiefs spread mats and deerskins and set out food, including two white loaves of a seed resembling rice. Munoz baptized twenty-three old women and three old men, and told the rest they must wait for a mission. Cook places the village on the east bank of the river in T 11 S, R 14 E, which is far more than three leagues from where he puts the camp; the pin follows the diary's three leagues. Cook adds that this was one of several villages on the lower San Joaquin effaced so thoroughly that modern informants gave ethnographers no indication they had ever existed.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 17.

stops.name: Bear Creek
stops.summary: North across the river and a league of high thick tules to a stream running east to west, with no running water, only pools, about sixty oaks and a few willows. Cutter reads this as Bear Creek rather than Mariposa Creek, since it is about three leagues south of the Merced, and Cook sees no reason to disagree.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 18.

stops.name: Merced River, west of Livingston
stops.summary: The Merced, reached east-north-east after about three leagues. Cook puts the northbound party on the river somewhere west of Livingston in T 6 S, R 11 E, and the other party east of Cressey. The village where the old woman was baptized was Chineguis; near by were Yunate, Chamuasi, Latelate and Lachuo. Cook counts a minimum of six villages in the stretch, averaging about 225 souls, and reckons the population between the San Joaquin and the foothills at fully two thousand.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 19.

stops.name: Tuolumne River (the Dolores)
stops.summary: Seven or eight leagues north-west to a big river, which the party named Our Lady of Sorrows for the day in September on which it had been sighted. Its banks were close together, the pasturage short and the soil saline. No Indians were found, but the signs of several villages and wide, heavily used trails were: word had evidently gone ahead from the Merced. Cook: the Tuolumne, according to the direction, near Modesto.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 20.

stops.name: Dry creek bed
stops.summary: About a league on in the same north-westerly direction, a creek bed full of sand with no water, which the diary judged could be a large river in the rains or the snowmelt. No oaks along its banks and few willows. Cook: undoubtedly Dry Creek, and the description is valid even today. Dry Creek runs north-east of the Tuolumne crossing rather than on the north-westerly line the diary gives, so the pin follows the line of march and the league stated, not the creek's course.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 21.

stops.name: Stanislaus River (the Guadalupe)
stops.summary: Two leagues further the party entered an oak forest about four leagues wide and of undetermined length, and a league and a half into it came on a river narrower than the others, its banks covered with wild grapevines, torote and ash. They named it Our Lady of Guadalupe and pitched a base camp. Cook: the Stanislaus; a party continuing north-west from near Modesto would have reached the river at or east of Ripon, where remnants of the valley oak forest can still be seen, perhaps a mile each side of the river and running unbroken from the San Joaquin junction east beyond Oakdale.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 22.

stops.name: Taulamne, below Knights Ferry
stops.summary: Six leagues east along the river to Taulamne, a village on steep cliffs the party could not climb; the people lived in caves and came down a pole held by one of them. Twelve or fifteen descended to a shelf in the rocks, carrying weapons, and accepted presents and pinole. Their reason for staying up was that soldiers killed and captured people. Cook: six leagues upstream of Ripon or Riverbank barely reaches the limestone bluffs just below Knights Ferry, which are unquestionably precipitous, and no place lower on the river could give the account's physical characteristics; the best guess is the vicinity of Knights Ferry.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 23.

stops.name: Calaveras River (the San Francisco)
stops.summary: About six leagues north-west to the bed of a big stream, dry, heavily overgrown with ash and wild vines, named the San Francisco for the saint's day on which it was found. Cutter identifies it with the Calaveras, and Cook sees little reason to disagree.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 25.

stops.name: Cosumnes River (the Pasion)
stops.summary: Nine leagues further in the same direction, a river of great volume which the party was told had already been found by an expedition looking for a land route to Bodega, and which carried that expedition's name, La Pasion. The people were affectionate and asked for a mission, but their language was wholly different and no interpreter could be had, so none were baptized. The party turned back the same day to the camp on the Stanislaus. Cutter identifies the river with the Cosumnes, and Cook notes that the distances fit and that the Miwok and Maidu language boundary runs along it. But Cook also objects that the diarist never mentions the Mokelumne, an all-year stream, and that a round trip of thirty leagues, about seventy-five miles, is incredible even for horsemen travelling without baggage; his alternative is that the two distances were both measured from the Stanislaus, which would end the day at the Mokelumne.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 25.

routes.notes: The far point of 4 October is drawn at the Cosumnes, which is Cutter's identification, but Cook objects that the day's thirty leagues are incredible and proposes the Mokelumne instead; the line beyond the Calaveras is a day excursion from the Stanislaus camp, not a stage of the march.

routes.label: Moraga and Munoz, southbound (4 October to 3 November 1806)
routes.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

stops.name: Base camp on the Stanislaus, the turn south
stops.summary: The party returned to the Guadalupe camp on the evening of its farthest day north and from here worked south, keeping close to the eastern edge of the valley along the Sierra foothills. Whether the far point of 4 October was the Cosumnes or the Mokelumne is unsettled; see the northbound route. On the fifteenth day, still at this camp, about forty armed Indians appeared, firing arrows into the air, with three coming forward as ambassadors carrying a flag made of a black ribbon of feathers with a red stripe down the middle.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

stops.name: Back across the Stanislaus and Tuolumne
stops.summary: On the sixteenth day camp was lifted from the Guadalupe and the party travelled to the Dolores; on the seventeenth it crossed from the Dolores to the Merced, both rivers it had named on the way north.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III.

stops.name: Mariposa Creek and the Chowchilla
stops.summary: Cutter identifies the diary's Santo Domingo with Mariposa Creek and its Tecolote, named for the owls that abounded there, with the Chowchilla.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 26.

stops.name: Fresno River (the Santa Ana)
stops.summary: Cook: the Santa Ana was the Fresno River. From the Merced to the San Joaquin the party stayed close to the eastern edge of the valley, where the streams are seasonal and permanent settlements were distinctly absent.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 27.

stops.name: Camp on the San Joaquin
stops.summary: The base camp on the San Joaquin, held from the twenty-second day to the twenty-fourth. Cook writes that Moraga probably halted approximately north of Fresno, below Le Grand; those two landmarks are some forty kilometres apart and do not agree, and the pin follows north of Fresno, which is the reading the southward march from the Fresno River supports.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 27.

stops.name: Pizcache (Pitkachi)
stops.summary: Pizcache, about 200 souls under a chief named Sujoyucomu, sighted by the party that scouted up the river on the twenty-third day; two old men and two old women were baptized. From this chief came the expedition's strangest testimony: that soldiers had come from the far side of the mountains about twenty years before, fought the Indians and killed many, that the sea lay ten days to the north beyond the range, and that to the south there was no sea but low hills. The chief said he had been present at the fight and had seen the ocean himself, and Munoz concluded that New Mexico lay very close to the other side of the Sierra. The diary places the village farther in the interior of the mountains, on the bank of the river. Cook's note on the name is a discrepancy: Kroeber has the Pitkachi holding the south side of the San Joaquin, 'living at Kohuou, near Herndon or Sycamore; at Weshiu, on a slough; and at Gewachiu, still farther downstream', and Gayton has Derby reaching Pitkachi country at the bend of the river in 1850, so Cook infers that the group moved downstream between 1806 and 1850. The pin follows the diary's foothills, not the ethnographers' valley floor.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 28.

stops.name: Kings River, near Sanger
stops.summary: Cook: the Kings River was reached near Sanger or Centerville. The village list at the end of the report names Aycayche and four others for the Kings River basin, while the text names Ayquiche and nine more, six upstream and three down, so the list does not include all the villages actually seen.

sources.citation: Munoz, Diary of the expedition made by Don Gabriel Moraga, Second Lieutenant of the Company of San Francisco, to the new discoveries in the Tulare Valley, 21 September to 2 November 1806, Santa Barbara Mission Archives IV: 1-47, trans. in Cook, Colonial Expeditions to the Interior of California: Central Valley, 1800-1820, Anthropological Records 16(6) (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1960), 239-292, chap. III n. 30.

stops.name: Kaweah delta and Telame
stops.summary: On the twenty-eighth day scouts reached the great oak forest along the Kaweah delta at or above Visalia, and the main party moved up on the twenty-ninth. The entry for the twenty-seventh day is missing from the report. The village of about 600 souls at which twenty-two people were baptized was Telame, the Telamni of the ethnographers, repeatedly mentioned by the early explorers. The water was very low, which Cook calls somewhat unusual for the region even in October. Munoz put the population of the lower Kaweah at 3,000; Cook holds that it probably reached a much higher figure.

III n. 33.

stops.name: Tule River, near Porterville
stops.summary: After a winding course of two days the party camped on the Tule River near the foothills, Cook thinks probably not far from Porterville.

III n. 36.

stops.name: Deer Creek
stops.summary: Cook: probably Deer Creek.

III n. 37.

stops.name: White River
stops.summary: Cook: probably White River.

III n. 38.

stops.name: Poso Creek
stops.summary: Cook: no distances are given, but from the description the most likely stream is Poso Creek.

stops.name: Kern River, above Bakersfield
stops.summary: Cook: the Kern River, probably some miles above Bakersfield.

stops.name: Kern River, the slough country
stops.summary: Cook: a long trip downstream would have brought the party into the slough country south of Bakersfield. Because Buenavista Lake is never mentioned, farther to the west, he holds it clear that Moraga did not get within sight of it, which is the lake Zalvidea had camped beside three months earlier.

stops.name: Grapevine Canyon
stops.summary: A sheltered place in the mountains with running water in a little creek and wild grapevines for almost the entire vegetation, reached just before sunset after the worst-worn horses had been sent off by another road. Munoz left the two villages seen that day undescribed, supposing that the Santa Barbara expedition would give a full account of them, and Cook notes that Zalvidea's report for August 1806 indeed did.

stops.name: Tejon Pass
stops.summary: On 1 November the party found the source of the stream, a grassy marsh, a valley of oaks and a lake of pure salt water, with a village to the east whose people the diary found too cunning in trading, and a second hidden among ravines and badlands whose people were away at a fiesta. Cook: on the last three days the party left the valley by way of Grapevine Canyon, over Tejon Pass, across the Tehachapi Mountains, which Cutter takes for the Santa Susanna Range, to San Fernando.

stops.name: Mission San Fernando
stops.summary: Arrival. On the last day the party followed the valley through mountains Munoz called indescribably rough, saw a light in the early evening and came upon the ranch of the fathers of San Fernando, reaching the mission itself the following day. Munoz signed the report on 2 November 1806, recording 141 baptisms on the expedition, all in extremis.
